title: Match Statements (Python's Switch)
summary: Branch on a value with match and case, Python's answer to the switch statement.
intro: Python had no switch statement until 3.10 added `match`. It checks one value against a list of cases and runs the first one that fits, with no fallthrough and no `break`.

steps.title: Matching literal values
steps.body:
`match` compares one value against a series of `case` patterns and runs the block of the first one that fits. It does the job of an `if`/`elif` chain that compares one variable with `==` again and again.

```python harness
code = 404
{{code}}
```

```python
match code:
    case 200:
        print("OK")
    case 404:
        print("Not Found")
    case _:
        print("Unknown status")
```

A literal pattern such as `200` or `"red"` matches when the value is equal to it, just like `==`. The underscore in `case _:` matches anything, so it works as the default. Put it last.

Unlike switch in C or Java, there is no fallthrough. At most one case block runs, then Python jumps past the whole `match`, so you never write `break`. If no case matches and there is no `case _:`, nothing runs and there is no error.

example.title: HTTP status messages
example.prompt: Turn the status codes 200, 404, and 999 into messages, with a default for codes it does not know.
example.code:
code = 200
match code:
    case 200:
        print(f"{code}: OK")
    case 404:
        print(f"{code}: Not Found")
    case _:
        print(f"{code}: Unknown status")

code = 404
match code:
    case 200:
        print(f"{code}: OK")
    case 404:
        print(f"{code}: Not Found")
    case _:
        print(f"{code}: Unknown status")

code = 999
match code:
    case 200:
        print(f"{code}: OK")
    case 404:
        print(f"{code}: Not Found")
    case _:
        print(f"{code}: Unknown status")
example.explanation: Each `match` checks `code` against the cases from the top. 200 and 404 hit their literal cases. 999 matches neither, so it lands in `case _:`. Only one block runs per `match`, which is why there is no `break`. The variable is reassigned before each copy of the `match` so every branch gets a turn.

practice.title: Traffic light actions
practice.prompt:
Map traffic light colors to an action with a match statement.

1. Set `color` to `"red"`, then match it: `"red"` prints `red: Stop`, `"green"` prints `green: Go`, and `case _:` prints the color followed by `: Unknown color`.
2. Reassign `color` to `"green"` and repeat the same match.
3. Reassign `color` to `"blue"` and repeat the same match.

Expected output:

```text
red: Stop
green: Go
blue: Unknown color
```
practice.starter:
color = "red"
# TODO: match color and print its action

color = "green"
# TODO: the same match again

color = "blue"
# TODO: the same match again
practice.solution:
color = "red"
match color:
    case "red":
        print(f"{color}: Stop")
    case "green":
        print(f"{color}: Go")
    case _:
        print(f"{color}: Unknown color")

color = "green"
match color:
    case "red":
        print(f"{color}: Stop")
    case "green":
        print(f"{color}: Go")
    case _:
        print(f"{color}: Unknown color")

color = "blue"
match color:
    case "red":
        print(f"{color}: Stop")
    case "green":
        print(f"{color}: Go")
    case _:
        print(f"{color}: Unknown color")

tests.output:
red: Stop
green: Go
blue: Unknown color

hints: Copy the shape of the status code example and swap the numbers for the strings `"red"` and `"green"`.
Use `f"{color}: Stop"` so the color appears at the start of the line.

steps.title: Alternatives with |
steps.body:
Join several patterns with `|` to run one block for any of them. Read `|` as "or". Inside a case you must write `|`: `case 6 or 7:` is a SyntaxError.

```python harness
day = 6
{{code}}
```

```python
match day:
    case 6 | 7:
        print("weekend")
    case 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5:
        print("weekday")
```

Cases are tried from top to bottom and the first match wins, so order matters when patterns overlap. Here `0` never reaches the second case:

```python harness
for n in [0, 1]:
    {{code}}
```

```python
match n:
    case 0:
        print("zero")
    case 0 | 1:
        print("zero or one")  # only 1 gets here
```

Python runs overlaps like that one without any warning. It only rejects a catch-all that sits above other cases: `case _:` there would swallow everything, so it is a SyntaxError:

```python
# case _:
# SyntaxError: wildcard makes remaining patterns unreachable
```

example.title: Weekend or weekday
example.prompt: Classify the day numbers 6, 3, and 9 as weekend, weekday, or invalid, where 1 to 5 are weekdays and 6 and 7 are the weekend.
example.code:
day = 6
match day:
    case 6 | 7:
        print(f"Day {day}: weekend")
    case 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5:
        print(f"Day {day}: weekday")
    case _:
        print(f"Day {day}: invalid")

day = 3
match day:
    case 6 | 7:
        print(f"Day {day}: weekend")
    case 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5:
        print(f"Day {day}: weekday")
    case _:
        print(f"Day {day}: invalid")

day = 9
match day:
    case 6 | 7:
        print(f"Day {day}: weekend")
    case 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5:
        print(f"Day {day}: weekday")
    case _:
        print(f"Day {day}: invalid")
example.output:
Day 6: weekend
Day 3: weekday
Day 9: invalid
example.explanation: `6 | 7` matches if `day` equals 6 or 7, so 6 hits the first case. 3 fails the first case and matches one of the five alternatives in the second. 9 fails both, so the cases run out and `case _:` takes it.

practice.title: File types
practice.prompt:
Classify file extensions with a match statement and alternatives.

1. Set `ext` to `"jpg"`, then match it: `"jpg"`, `"png"`, or `"gif"` print the extension followed by `: image`, `"txt"` or `"md"` print it followed by `: text`, and anything else prints it followed by `: other`.
2. Reassign `ext` to `"md"` and repeat the same match.
3. Reassign `ext` to `"exe"` and repeat the same match.

Expected output:

```text
jpg: image
md: text
exe: other
```
practice.starter:
ext = "jpg"
# TODO: match ext and print its kind

ext = "md"
# TODO: the same match again

ext = "exe"
# TODO: the same match again
practice.solution:
ext = "jpg"
match ext:
    case "jpg" | "png" | "gif":
        print(f"{ext}: image")
    case "txt" | "md":
        print(f"{ext}: text")
    case _:
        print(f"{ext}: other")

ext = "md"
match ext:
    case "jpg" | "png" | "gif":
        print(f"{ext}: image")
    case "txt" | "md":
        print(f"{ext}: text")
    case _:
        print(f"{ext}: other")

ext = "exe"
match ext:
    case "jpg" | "png" | "gif":
        print(f"{ext}: image")
    case "txt" | "md":
        print(f"{ext}: text")
    case _:
        print(f"{ext}: other")

tests.output:
jpg: image
md: text
exe: other

hints: One case can list several strings: `case "jpg" | "png" | "gif":`.
Use `case "txt" | "md":` for text and `case _:` for the rest.

steps.title: Captures and guards
steps.body:
A bare name in a case is a capture pattern. It matches any value and binds it to that name, so the block can use it:

```python harness
speed = 50
{{code}}
```

```python
match speed:
    case s:
        print(f"OK at {s}")
```

Add a guard with `if` after the pattern to match only when a condition is true. Python binds the name, checks the guard, and moves on to the next case if it is false.

```python harness
SPEED_LIMIT = 120

for speed in [130, 50]:
    match speed:
        {{code}}
        case s:
            print(f"OK at {s}")
```

```python
case s if s > SPEED_LIMIT:
    print(f"Speeding at {s}")
```

The big gotcha: a bare name always captures, even when a variable with that name exists. `case SPEED_LIMIT:` does not compare with the constant. It matches everything and rebinds `SPEED_LIMIT`. Python rejects it when more cases follow:

```python
# case SPEED_LIMIT:
# SyntaxError: name capture 'SPEED_LIMIT' makes remaining patterns unreachable
```

As the last case it is allowed, and it silently overwrites the constant with the value. To compare with a constant, capture and guard: `case s if s == SPEED_LIMIT:`. A final unguarded capture works like `case _:` but also hands you the value by name.

example.title: Speed check
example.prompt: Compare the speeds 130, 120, and 50 with a speed limit of 120 using guarded capture patterns.
example.code:
SPEED_LIMIT = 120

speed = 130
match speed:
    case s if s > SPEED_LIMIT:
        print(f"Speeding at {s}")
    case s if s == SPEED_LIMIT:
        print(f"At the limit: {s}")
    case s:
        print(f"OK at {s}")

speed = 120
match speed:
    case s if s > SPEED_LIMIT:
        print(f"Speeding at {s}")
    case s if s == SPEED_LIMIT:
        print(f"At the limit: {s}")
    case s:
        print(f"OK at {s}")

speed = 50
match speed:
    case s if s > SPEED_LIMIT:
        print(f"Speeding at {s}")
    case s if s == SPEED_LIMIT:
        print(f"At the limit: {s}")
    case s:
        print(f"OK at {s}")
example.output:
Speeding at 130
At the limit: 120
OK at 50
example.explanation: Every case captures the speed as `s`. For 130 the first guard `s > SPEED_LIMIT` is true. For 120 it is false, so Python tries the next case, whose guard compares with the constant through `==`. For 50 both guards fail and the last `case s:` catches it like a default, with the value in hand.

practice.title: Temperature labels
practice.prompt:
Label temperatures with guarded capture patterns.

1. Keep the constants `FREEZING = 0` and `HOT = 30`.
2. Set `temp` to `-3`, then match it: capture it as `t` and print `t` followed by `: Freezing` if it is below `FREEZING`, followed by `: Hot` if it is above `HOT`, and use a final `case t:` that prints it followed by `: Mild`.
3. Reassign `temp` to `18` and repeat the same match.
4. Reassign `temp` to `40` and repeat the same match.

Expected output:

```text
-3: Freezing
18: Mild
40: Hot
```
practice.starter:
FREEZING = 0
HOT = 30

temp = -3
# TODO: match temp with guarded captures and print its label

temp = 18
# TODO: the same match again

temp = 40
# TODO: the same match again
practice.solution:
FREEZING = 0
HOT = 30

temp = -3
match temp:
    case t if t < FREEZING:
        print(f"{t}: Freezing")
    case t if t > HOT:
        print(f"{t}: Hot")
    case t:
        print(f"{t}: Mild")

temp = 18
match temp:
    case t if t < FREEZING:
        print(f"{t}: Freezing")
    case t if t > HOT:
        print(f"{t}: Hot")
    case t:
        print(f"{t}: Mild")

temp = 40
match temp:
    case t if t < FREEZING:
        print(f"{t}: Freezing")
    case t if t > HOT:
        print(f"{t}: Hot")
    case t:
        print(f"{t}: Mild")
hints: Start with `case t if t < FREEZING:`.
Never write `case HOT:`. A bare name captures everything. Compare in a guard instead: `case t if t > HOT:`.
The last case is a plain `case t:` with no guard.

recap:
- `match value:` tries each `case` from top to bottom and runs only the first match.
- `case 200:` and `case "red":` match literal values with `==`.
- `case _:` is the default. Put it last.
- No fallthrough, so no `break`.
- `case 6 | 7:` matches any of several alternatives.
- `case n:` captures the value into `n`, and `case n if n < 0:` adds a guard.
- A bare name always captures. Compare with a constant in a guard: `case s if s == LIMIT:`.
- `if`/`elif` chains, and dictionary lookups from a later lesson, are the older ways to branch on a value.
